[warm] Clean hands, clean food. [short pause] The first rule of the kitchen.

[friendly] Welcome to Kitchen Fundamentals. [short pause] This is part one of a ten-part series on cooking basics.

[serious] Here's the short version. [short pause] Most food poisoning at home is carried by hands, not by exotic ingredients. [short pause] Wash with soap for at least twenty seconds, at the right moments. Keep sick people out of the kitchen. Tie back your hair. Cover any cuts. And use a clean spoon every time you taste. [short pause] Everything else in this series builds on that.


[long pause] [curious] So, why does hygiene come first?

Because cooking is applied biology. [short pause] Bacteria, viruses and parasites ride into your food on hands, on sneezes, on rings... [short pause] and on phone screens.

[quietly] You can't see most of them. You can't smell them. [short pause] You can't taste them. [short pause] And cooking doesn't always save you. [short pause] Salads, bread, garnishes and leftovers are often eaten without any more heat.

[warm] The cheapest, most effective food safety tool ever invented? [short pause] Soap and running water.


[long pause] [friendly] Let's talk about how to wash your hands properly.

First, wet your hands with clean running water. Warm or cold, either is fine.

Second, lather up with soap. [short pause] Backs of your hands, between your fingers, your thumbs, and under your nails.

Third, scrub for at least twenty seconds. [chuckles] The classic timer? Humming a short song, twice.

Fourth, rinse under running water.

And fifth, dry with a clean towel or a paper towel. [short pause] Damp hands spread germs more easily than dry ones.

[short pause] A quick word on hand sanitizer. [serious] It's a backup, not a replacement. It doesn't work well on greasy or visibly dirty hands, and it doesn't remove everything soap does.


[long pause] [friendly] So, when should you wash?

Before you start cooking, and every time you come back to the kitchen.

After handling raw meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, or unwashed produce.

After touching the bin, a pet, your phone, your face or hair, money, or cleaning chemicals.

After using the bathroom, coughing, sneezing, or blowing your nose.

And between tasks, especially when you switch from raw food to ready-to-eat food.

[short pause] [lighthearted] If in doubt, wash. [short pause] [chuckles] It takes less time than reading this sentence twice.


[long pause] [serious] Now, an important one. [short pause] Cook healthy, or don't cook.

If you have vomiting or diarrhea, let someone else cook. [short pause] And keep it that way for at least forty-eight hours after your symptoms stop.

[quietly] Some of the most contagious stomach viruses spread easily through food, and they survive well on surfaces. [short pause] [warm] A professional kitchen sends sick staff home. A home kitchen should do the same.


[long pause] [friendly] Finally, a few small habits that add up.

Keep your hair tied back. Take your jewelry off. [short pause] Rings and watches trap food and bacteria.

Cover cuts with a waterproof dressing, ideally a brightly colored one, and add a glove on that hand.

Keep one towel for your hands and a different one for dishes, and change them often.

When you taste, use a clean spoon every time. [short pause] [playful] Never, ever, put the tasting spoon back in the pot.

And your phone? [short pause] It goes everywhere your hands go. [short pause] Keep it out of the cooking area, or wash your hands after touching it.


[long pause] [reflective] Why does this outlast any technology?

Appliances will get smarter. Ingredients will be delivered faster. [short pause] But food will always be prepared by someone's hands, and microbes will always be invisible.

[warm] A twenty-second habit beats any gadget.

[short pause] [excited] Tomorrow, we tackle the single most important number in food safety... [short pause] the danger zone.

[friendly] See you then.
